## Pareto Optimal Plans {#sec-algorithm}

::: {.section-subtitle}
Computing the Pareto front exactly, its complexity, and the ZenoSolver with its certificates and their verification
:::

We now focus on finding the Pareto Optimal Plans from the lists of $2t - p$ cities, for the
symmetric case: (S) holds throughout, and the statements about the front also need the hub
triangles (H), which (A1) and (AΔ) imply. This section corresponds to §6 to §8 of the
[theory note](https://github.com/aquemy/ZenoSolver/blob/master/doc/theory/exact-front.md). The
[algorithm page](../solver/algorithm.qmd) of the Solver section describes how the implementation
carries out each step.

### Definitions {#sec-definitions}

**Cost of a list**: Given a list $X$ of $2t - p$ cities, the cost of any plan using only the
cities in $X$ is uniquely defined by $c(X) = \sum_{i \in X} c_i$.

**Makespan of a list**: The makespan of a list is that of the shortest schedule that uses its
cities in a feasible way. Only the least largest load $M(X) = \min \max_k \ell(X_k)$ over the
admissible partitions of $X$ matters: by Theorem 4.1 it is the makespan of a plan, and by
Theorem 4.5, under (H), the Pareto front is the Pareto set of the pairs $(c(X), M(X))$.

The list $X$ does not hold any information about which plane will land in a particular city, and
choosing the partition is the hard part.

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Theorem 7.1" >}} **3-Partition reduction.** Let $a_1, \dots, a_{3m}$ and $B$ be natural
numbers with $\sum_i a_i = mB$ and $B/4 < a_i < B/2$ for every $i$. In the symmetric instance with
one city of duration $a_i$ for each $i$, $p = m$ planes and $t = 2m$ passengers, the list $X$ that
lands once in every city has $M(X) \le 2B$ if and only if the $a_i$ split into $m$ triples of sum
$B$.
:::

::: {.sketch}
*Sketch.* Every city lies in one group, so by {{< node "Lemma 2.3" badge=false >}} the admissible
partitions of $X$ are those into odd groups, and odd groups of duration at most $B$ summing to $mB$
must be triples ({{< node "Theorem 7.1" text="full proof" badge=false >}}).
:::

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Proposition 7.2" >}} **Partition reduction, $p = 2$.** Let $a_1, \dots, a_m$ be natural
numbers with sum $2B$, $r \ge m$ odd and $K = B + 1$. In the symmetric instance with $2r$ cities,
of durations $a_i + K$ for $i \le m$ and $K$ for the other $2r - m$, $p = 2$ and $t = r + 1$, the
list $X$ that lands once in every city has $M(X) \le 2(B + rK)$ if and only if some sub-multiset
of the $a_i$ sums to $B$. All durations are positive.
:::

*Remark (hardness, from the literature).* 3-Partition is strongly NP-complete and Partition is
NP-complete [[GJ79](#ref-GJ79)]. The instance of Theorem 7.1 has the numbers $a_i$, $B$ and $m$
of the 3-Partition instance, and both instances are written down in polynomial time. Granted these
cited results, deciding $M(X) \le 2T$, with $d$, $X$, $p$ and $T$ as input, is strongly NP-hard
when $p$ is part of the input, by Theorem 7.1, and stays NP-hard for $p = 2$, by Proposition 7.2.
In particular, unless P = NP, no polynomial algorithm, such as a greedy distribution of the
durations of a list into $p$ planes, computes $M(X)$ for every list $X$. The hardness results are
cited, not formalised.

The greedies of both earlier papers do miss front points. Both fix a list of landings, a *possibly
Pareto-optimal plan* (PPP), and schedule it greedily, giving the longest durations first to the
least-loaded plane: [[QS15](#ref-QS15)] in its Algorithm 1, the 2023 version of this paper in its
§3.2. They state the greedy in two forms. *EvoCOP's greedy* $G_E$ takes a PPP of $t$ eastbound and
$t - p$ westbound landings and a set $\beta$ of P3 patterns, landings common to both. Loop 1: while
westbound landings outside $\beta$ remain, the least-loaded plane flies the longest remaining
eastbound landing outside $\beta$ if it is in $C_I$, and the longest remaining westbound one
otherwise. Loop 2: each remaining eastbound landing, longest first, goes to the least-loaded plane
in $C_I$. Then each P3 pattern in $C_i$, longest first, adds $2d_i$ to each of the two least-loaded
planes. The makespan of the PPP is the largest load, the least over the sets $\beta$. *The 2023
greedy* $G_A$ takes a PPP of $k + p$ patterns $A$, $k$ patterns $\bar A$ and $t - p - k$ pairs of
patterns $B$ and $\bar B$: each pair, longest first, adds $2d$ to the least-loaded plane; the $p$
longest patterns $A$, in decreasing order, go to the least-loaded planes that have none yet; while
crossings remain, the least-loaded plane whose next pattern ($\bar A$ after $A$, $A$ after $\bar A$)
is still available takes the longest remaining one of that type; then the pairs are dealt again.
The papers do not say how ties of "least-loaded" are broken.

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Proposition 4.8" >}} **The papers' greedies are not exact.** *(a)* For
$d = \bar d = (6, 10)$, $c = (40, 20)$, $t = 5$, $p = 2$ and every table of flights between central
cities, $(260, 60) \in \mathcal F$, yet for every PPP of cost at most 260, $G_E$ (for every set
$\beta$ and every tie-breaking) and $G_A$ (for every tie-breaking) give a makespan above 60. On the
landings of $(260, 60)$, five in $C_1$ and three in $C_2$, loops 1 and 2 without P3 patterns end
with the loads 52 and 68, and every $\beta$ gives at least 64.

*(b)* For $d = \bar d = (1, 3)$, $c = (9, 5)$, $t = 4$, $p = 2$ and every table of flights between
central cities, $(42, 12) \in \mathcal F$, and for every PPP of cost at most 42, $G_A$ gives a
makespan above 12 for every tie-breaking. $G_E$ reaches $(42, 12)$: the PPP of eastbound landings
$C_1, C_1, C_2, C_2$ and westbound landings $C_1, C_2$, of cost 42, with one P3 pattern in $C_2$,
gets makespan 12 for every tie-breaking.
:::

In (a), the greedy gives each plane a pattern $A$ in the slow city $C_2$ first, while the groups
$\{10, 10, 10\}$ and $\{6, 6, 6, 6, 6\}$, both odd and hence admissible, both last 60. The
experiment [E10](#sec-e10) measures how often $G_E$ is exact.

The method below never computes $M(X)$ for a fixed list. It sweeps the makespans instead, and
computes for each one the least cost over all lists at once.

### Computing the Pareto front {#sec-breakpoints}

For an integer *level* $T \ge 0$ let
$$E(T) = \min\{c(X) : |X| = 2t - p,\ X_1, \dots, X_p \text{ admissible},\ \delta(X_k) \le T \text{ for all } k\},$$
the least cost of an admissible partition whose loads are all at most $2T$ ($\infty$ if there is
none).

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Lemma 6.2" >}} **The function $E$.** $E$ is non-increasing and attained when finite.
With $1 \le p$, $E(T) = \infty$ for $T < d_{\min}\kappa$. A level $T$ at which $E$ drops
($E(T) = C$ and $E(T') > C$ for every $T' < T$) has $T \le (2t - p)\,d_{\max}$.
:::

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Proposition 6.3" >}} **Front = breakpoints of $E$.** Assume (S), (H) and $p \le t$.
Then $(C, M) \in \mathcal F$ if and only if $M = 2T$ for some level $T$ with $E(T) = C$ and
$E(T') > C$ for every $T' < T$.
:::

The Pareto front is read off the levels where $E$ drops, and only a bounded range of levels
matters. At both ends, every plan obeys a lower bound.

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Proposition 3.6" >}} **Lower bounds.** Let $p \le t$. Every feasible plan costs at least
$(2t - p)\,c_{\min}$. Under (S) and $1 \le p$, every feasible plan has makespan at least
$2 d_{\min}\kappa$.
:::

::: {.sketch}
*Sketch.* The $p$ non-empty groups of Lemma 3.5 have $2t - p$ landings in all, and one of them has
at least $\kappa = \lceil (2t - p)/p \rceil$
({{< node "Proposition 3.6" text="full proof" badge=false >}}).
:::

On the [example instance](#fig-plan) ($2t - p = 4$, $\kappa = 2$, $d_{\min} = 2$), $E$ is infinite
below level 4, and it reaches the least cost $(2t - p)\,c_{\min} = 4$ at level 10:

| $T$ | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 8 | 9 | 10 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $E(T)$ | 36 | 30 | 24 | 20 | 14 | 14 | 4 |
| front point | $(36, 8)$ | $(30, 10)$ | $(24, 12)$ | $(20, 14)$ | $(14, 16)$ | none | $(4, 20)$ |

: $E$ on the example instance, computed by enumeration; $L = E$ at every level. Level 9 is not a breakpoint, so the front has no point of makespan 18. {#tbl-levels}

A city dominated by another is never needed ({{< node "Proposition 6.5" >}}): if
$d_{i'} \le d_i$ and $c_{i'} \le c_i$, replacing the landings in $C_i$ of an admissible partition by
landings in $C_{i'}$ gives an admissible partition with the same group sizes and no larger cost or
loads. The exact programs below use the non-dominated cities only.

**One-plane table.** Everything is built from the cheapest group of a single plane.

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Lemma 6.1" >}} Let $G[0][\tau] = 0$ and
$$G[m + 1][\tau] = \min_{i : d_i \le \tau}\big(c_i + G[m][\tau - d_i]\big),$$
$\infty$ over the empty set. Then $G[m][\tau]$ is the least cost of a multiset of $m$ cities of
total duration at most $\tau$, and it is $\infty$ if and only if there is none; the memoised table
agrees with it.
:::

**Bounds.** Bounds on $E(T)$ combine *gadgets*, small sets of planes with their groups, by a
knapsack over planes and landings. Single planes of any size give the relaxation $L$ of Lemma 3.5.
Single planes of odd size and *pairs*, two even planes linked by one $(B\bar B)$-pairing in a
non-dominated city, give an upper bound $U$.

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Proposition 6.4" >}} **Bracket.** At every level $T$ of the table,
$L(T) \le E(T) \le U(T)$, and where $L(T) = U(T)$, $E(T) = L(T)$.
:::

**The link-forest dynamic program.** When the bracket $L \le E \le U$ does not close, $E(T)$ is
computed exactly by building the trees of a link forest from the leaves up: a table of child
items (a pairing with the subtree hanging from it), a table of subtrees hanging from a parent
pairing, a table of rooted trees, and a knapsack that combines trees into a forest of $p$ planes
and $2t - p$ landings, the free landings of each plane being filled from $G$, and the labels of the
links being the non-dominated cities.

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Theorem 6.7" >}} For $1 \le p$, the link-forest dynamic program returns $E(T)$ at every
level $T$ of the table.
:::

::: {.sketch}
*Sketch.* Every finite entry is the cost of a structure satisfying (F1) and (F2), whose groups
are admissible by {{< node "Lemma 2.6" >}}; conversely, the rooted link forest of an optimal
partition, moved to the non-dominated cities by Proposition 6.5, is bounded below entry by entry
({{< node "Theorem 6.7" text="full proof" badge=false >}}).
:::

**The σ-DP.** A second exact program works on parity matrices directly. By
{{< node "Lemma 2.7" >}}, an admissible partition of $2t - p$ cities has a parity matrix touching
at most $w = \min(p - 1, t - p)$ cities. The *σ-graph* has nodes $(k, j, \sigma)$: $k$ planes
processed, $j$ landings used, and $\sigma$ the set of cities marked an odd number of times so far,
of size at most $w$. An arc adds a plane with $m$ landings and a set $\eta$ of at most $w$ marked
non-dominated cities, with $|\eta| + 1 \le m$, $|\eta| \equiv m + 1 \pmod 2$ and at most $w$ cities
in $\sigma \triangle \eta$, weighted by $c(\eta)$ plus the cheapest filler from $G$.

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Theorem 6.8" >}} **σ-DP.** Let $1 \le p \le t$. At every level $T$ of the table, the
shortest path from $(0, 0, \emptyset)$ to $(p, 2t - p, \emptyset)$ in the σ-graph has weight
$E(T)$.
:::

The verified solver of the [Verification](#sec-verification) section chooses between the two
exact programs by an estimate of their cost.

**Constructing the plan.** For each front point, a partition attaining $E(T)$ is rebuilt from the
choices of the exact program, a link forest is computed from it as in the proof of Lemma 2.6, and
the plan is built as in {{< node "Theorem 4.1" >}}.

**Complexity.** The steps of the link-forest program are counted in Lean.

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Theorem 7.3" >}} **Step count.** *(a)* At every level $T$, the link-forest program with
a step counter returns the value of the program, which is $E(T)$ when $1 \le p$ and $T$ is a level
of the table, in at most $P(n, t, p, T) = 30\,(n + 1)^2(p + 1)^2(t + 1)^2(T + 1)$ steps.
*(b)* With $1 \le p \le t$, building $G$ once for the levels $0, \dots, T_{\rm top} = (2t - p)\,d_{\max}$
and running the counted program at each of them returns the front of the verified solver in at
most $(T_{\rm top} + 1)\,P(n, t, p, T_{\rm top})$ steps, the table included.
:::

A step is one iteration of a minimum loop, one cell of a table, one element scanned by a
membership test, or one level of the scan. So $E(T)$ and the front take a number of steps
polynomial in $n$, $t$, $p$ and the largest level $(2t - p)\,d_{\max}$: pseudo-polynomial in the
durations, while computing $M(X)$ for a fixed list is as hard as 3-Partition (Theorem 7.1 and the
remark above).

### ZenoSolver {#sec-zenosolver}

ZenoSolver is a C++ software dedicated to generate and exactly solve MultiZenoTravel instances.
ZenoSolver computes the Pareto Front using the algorithm described in this section, and returns
it with a certificate, so that it need not be trusted. It outputs the corresponding PDDL file, that
can be directly used by most AI planners.

For a symmetric instance, it reduces the instance (gcd of the durations, dominated cities),
computes the range of levels and $G$, evaluates $L$ and $U$ on every level, and runs an exact
program only on the levels the bracket leaves open. Some of its shortcuts are optimisations that
this paper does not prove: it takes $U$ as exact when $p \le 2$ or $t \le p + 1$, adds an upper
bound $U_3$ over chains of three planes, and builds link trees of at most $\min(p, t - p + 1)$
planes; the certificate of each run checks the front it prints. As $E$ is non-increasing,
$E(a) = E(b)$ for $a < b$ fixes $E$ on $[a, b]$, which allows bisection over runs of open levels.
A plan is then built and simulated for every front point. For a non-symmetric instance, it
brackets the front between lower bounds and achieved plans, and closes the gaps by a search over
scheduled configurations, as described in the [non-symmetric section](#sec-ns-front).

With each front, ZenoSolver can write a certificate that a checker verifies without trusting it,
and the Lean development contains a solver of its own, proved correct
([Verification](#sec-verification)). The experiment [E7](#sec-e7) and the
[benchmark suites](#sec-bench) report the performances of the C++ solver.

### Certificates {#sec-certificates}

A Pareto front is a strong claim: no plan, among infinitely many, beats any of its points. A
certificate reduces the claim to finitely many checks that a program much simpler than the solver
can run. For a symmetric instance and a list $(C_1, M_1), \dots, (C_r, M_r)$ with
$M_1 < \dots < M_r$ and $C_1 > \dots > C_r$, a checker verifies four obligations:

1. every listed point has a plan, which the checker simulates: feasible, of cost $C_i$ and
   makespan $M_i$;
2. no plan has makespan below $M_1$: the checker verifies $M_1 = 2 d_{\min}\kappa$
   (Proposition 3.6);
3. for every $i < r$, every plan of makespan below $M_{i+1}$ costs at least $C_i$: the checker
   establishes a lower bound of at least $C_i$ at the level
   $T^\star_i = \lfloor \lfloor (M_{i+1} - 1)/2 \rfloor / g \rfloor$, with $g$ the gcd of the
   durations;
4. no plan costs less than $C_r$: the checker verifies $C_r = (2t - p)\,c_{\min}$
   (Proposition 3.6).

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Theorem 8.1" >}} **Obligations imply the front.** Let $\mathcal S$ be a set of points
and $(C_1, M_1), \dots, (C_r, M_r)$, $r \ge 1$, with $M_1 < \dots < M_r$ and
$C_1 > \dots > C_r$. If (1) every listed point is in $\mathcal S$, (2) every point of
$\mathcal S$ has makespan at least $M_1$, (3) for $i < r$ every point of $\mathcal S$ with
makespan below $M_{i+1}$ has cost at least $C_i$, and (4) every point of $\mathcal S$ has cost at
least $C_r$, then the list is the Pareto front of $\mathcal S$.
:::

::: {.sketch}
*Sketch.* Every point of $\mathcal S$ lies at or after $M_1$, so it falls in some interval
$[M_i, M_{i+1})$ or after $M_r$, where obligation 3 or 4 bounds its cost by $C_i$; the listed
points are pairwise incomparable ({{< node "Theorem 8.1" text="full proof" badge=false >}}).
With $\mathcal S = \mathcal A$, {{< node "Lemma 1.7" badge=false >}} then gives
$\mathcal F = \{(C_i, M_i) : 1 \le i \le r\}$.
:::

The work of the checker is obligation 3. A gap of kind `relaxed` recomputes $L(T^\star_i)$, a
lower bound under (S) alone by Lemma 3.5, whatever the flights between central cities. A gap of
kind `forest` recomputes $E(T^\star_i)$ with the checker's own exact programs, a lower bound under
(H) by Theorem 4.4. On 400 random instances, all but 15 of 5,277 gaps close with `relaxed`, so 386
of the 400 fronts are certified by the relaxation alone.

For non-symmetric instances the format has a version 2, whose gap kinds rest on the results of the
[non-symmetric section](#sec-nonsymmetric): `relaxed`, the relaxation of Lemma 3.5 with the weight
$e$; `roles`, `lagrangian` and `balanced`, lower bounds on the role configurations
({{< node "Proposition 8.3" >}}, {{< node "Proposition 8.4" >}}, {{< node "Proposition 8.5" >}});
and `search`, for the gaps that waiting leaves open ({{< node "Proposition 8.6" >}}). The
[certificate format](../solver/certificates.qmd) page describes the files.

#### Verification {#sec-verification}

A certificate moves the trust from the solver to the checker, and the checker to a theorem.
Two checkers implement the obligations: `zeno check`, in C++, and `zeno-check`, compiled from
Lean. Both print the assumptions a certificate relied on, among (S), (A1) or (AΔ), and (A1-NS).

**The Lean checker.** Its soundness is a theorem for each version of the format.

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Theorem 8.2" >}} **Version 1 checker.** If `Cert.check` accepts a certificate of format
version 1, its points are the Pareto front of the feasible plans of its instance for every table
of flights between central cities satisfying (H), and for every table if all its gaps are
`relaxed`. The same holds for the plans with rational or real times (Lemma 1.3) and, for every
table satisfying (H), for the plans whose planes end anywhere.
:::

In Lean, these are `Cert.check_sound_hub`, `Cert.check_sound_relaxed`, `Cert.check_sound_rat_hub`
and `Cert.check_sound_anywhere_hub`, with the corollaries `Cert.check_sound_A1` under (A1) and
`Cert.check_sound_ATri` under (AΔ).

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Theorem 8.7" >}} **Version 2 checker.** If `Cert2.check` accepts a certificate of format
version 2, its points are the Pareto front of the feasible plans of its instance, for every table
of flights between central cities that satisfies (A1-NS) if the certificate lists (A1-NS), and for
every table otherwise.
:::

On the 66 certificates the C++ solver writes for the benchmark suite, up to 3.9 MB and 240,000
legs, the compiled Lean checker accepts every one, in 33 ms at the median and 2.3 s at most.

**The verified solver.** `zeno-front` is a solver of its own, written in Lean, with a proof that
its output is the Pareto front.

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Theorem 6.9" >}} **Verified solver.** Assume (S), (H) and $1 \le p \le t$. The list
`solveFront d c t p` is the Pareto front of the feasible plans.
:::

In Lean, this is `solveFront_isParetoFront_hub`, with the corollaries `solveFront_isParetoFront`
under (A1) and `solveFront_isParetoFront_ATri` under (AΔ). The solver lists, by increasing
makespan, the points $(E(T), 2T)$ at which $E$ drops, found by splitting intervals of the levels
from $d_{\min}\kappa$ to $(2t - p)\,d_{\max}$; at each level it takes $L(T)$ where $L(T) = U(T)$
(Proposition 6.4), and otherwise runs the link-forest program (Theorem 6.7) or the σ-DP
(Theorem 6.8), whichever its cost estimate prefers. It solves the 66 instances of the benchmark
suite, 0.04 s at the median and 10 s at most, and its fronts equal those of the C++ solver, which
continuous integration checks on the golden instances.

**What is trusted.** A machine-checked statement is a Lean theorem whose axioms are among
`propext`, `Classical.choice` and `Quot.sound`, which an audit of every declaration reads when the
site is built. The executables add the Lean compiler and the code that parses the files, which is
not verified. The badges of this paper come from the claim ledger of the repository, which badges a
statement machine-checked only when Lean proves every assertion of it, and from that audit. The
C++ solver is not verified; its fronts are checked through certificates. The experiment
[E8](#sec-e8) tests both checkers against thousands of corrupted certificates.
